slides.title: We tested a margin-first hypothesis against seven conditions: the diagnosis held, but the first answer was not enough to reach 3.0%

claims.claim: Starting hypothesis: the margin loss is a gross-margin and delivery-economics problem, not a wage problem — resetting promotions and repricing delivery, rather than cutting labour, would restore 3.0%.
1. The decline is driven mainly by gross margin and e-commerce, not wages — Supported
evidence: Margin bridge FY2023–25: gross margin −1.02 pts and e-commerce fulfilment −0.84 pts = 79% of the fall; store labour −0.30 pts = 13% (p.5)

claims.claim: 2. Extra promotion is not buying profitable traffic — Supported
evidence: 38% of FY2025 events lost money; the +5-pt rise in promo share costs $10.5M a year and would need ~$53M of new sales to pay back (p.6–7)

claims.claim: 3. E-commerce loses money once fully costed — Supported
evidence: With third-party delivery and 70% cannibalisation: −$10.4M in FY2025; −$12.34 per delivered order, −$1.64 per click-and-collect order (p.9)

claims.claim: 4. Delivery can be repriced without losing the customer base — Partly
evidence: Fee test: delivered orders −9%, click-and-collect +14%, e-commerce sales only −2%; worth ~$2.5M a year — but only a quarter of the loss (p.13)

claims.claim: 5. Store hours can be cut 8% without raising shrink or hurting service (management view) — Not supported
evidence: Leanest-labour quartile runs 3.1% shrink vs 2.3% in the richest; shrink rose 0.5 pts as hours per $1,000 of sales fell 6% (p.8)

claims.claim: 6. Weak stores can be exited within the board's commitments — Supported
evidence: 6 of the 9 negative-EBITDA stores have leases ending by 2027, so no vote is needed; exit adds ~$4.4M a year (p.14)

claims.claim: 7. The levers in the starting hypothesis are enough for 3.0% within $25M — Not supported
evidence: Promotions + delivery give ~$13M; even all seven firm levers give ~$30M → ~2.6%; ~$5M more must come from a second wave (p.15)

claims.claim: Revised answer: the diagnosis holds, but promotions and delivery alone are not enough — the plan adds shrink, targeted labour and store exits, and needs a prepared second wave to reach 3.0%.

slides.title: Gross margin and e-commerce fulfilment explain ~80% of the 2.35-point margin decline; store labour explains only 13%

evidence: Operating margin 3.37% (FY2023) → 1.02% (FY2025)

E-commerce fulfilment −0.84 pts, −$12.6M, 36%

Other SG&A 0.00, 0.0, 0%

evidence: Labour had the largest dollar rise (+$14.3M), but sales grew 5.8%
At FY2023's 11.8% ratio, FY2025 labour would have cost $177.4M — so only $4.5M is excess
E-commerce fulfilment more than tripled: $5.2M → $18.1M

slides.title: The 1.0-point gross-margin loss is fully explained by more promotion and more shrink; private label offset less than a fifth of it

claims.claim: The 1.0-point gross-margin loss is fully explained by more promotion and more shrink; private label offset less than a fifth of it
evidence: Promotion mix: Promo share 24.0% → 29.0% (+5.0 pts) × −14 pts margin gap = −0.70 pts, −$10.5M
Shrink: 2.1% → 2.6% of sales (+0.5 pts) = −0.50 pts, −$7.5M
Private label: Share 17.0% → 18.5% (+1.5 pts) × +12 pts margin gap = +0.18 pts, +$2.7M
Total explained −1.02, −15.3; Actual change 26.04% → 25.02% −1.02, −15.3

claims.claim: Harlow is also funding more of each promotion itself
evidence: Vendor funding covered 55% of markdowns in FY2023 but only 46% in FY2025

claims.claim: Shrink is now 2.6% of sales ($39.1M)
evidence: produce waste 45%, theft 35%, admin and receiving errors 20%

slides.title: Deeper promotion has not paid for itself: 38% of events lose money, and the extra promo share would need ~$53M of new sales to break even

claims.claim: 38% of FY2025 promotional events lost money even after counting the extra units they sold
evidence: 55% → 46% share of markdowns funded by vendors, FY2023 → FY2025
~$53M of new sales needed (at 20¢ contribution) to repay the $10.5M a year that +5 pts of promo share costs (0.70 pts × $1,503M ÷ 0.20)

claims.claim: Testing the claim that “promotions work”: at the chain's depth the comp gain repays less than half its cost
evidence: Category team: the deepest-promo stores grew comps +1.8% vs +0.2% for the rest.
Benefit: +1.6 pts of sales × 20¢ = 0.32 pts of sales in contribution
Cost: every extra point of promo share costs 0.14 pts of sales in margin
Break-even: those stores can carry at most 0.32 ÷ 0.14 = 2.3 pts more promo share
The chain added 5 pts; at that depth the comp gain repays less than half its cost (0.32 vs 0.70 pts)
And it is correlation: stores were not chosen at random

claims.claim: Broad promotional depth is an expensive and weak defence; private label (+12 pts margin) and fresh are better ones
evidence: ValuMart has opened 11 stores in Harlow trade areas; nearby Harlow stores ran comps of −4.2% vs +1.1%
Despite more promotion, “more expensive” perception rose from 33% to 41%
Customers choose Harlow for fresh produce (58%) and convenience (44%), not price

claims.claim: Implication: cut the loss-making events chain-wide, require vendor funding as a condition of each event, keep targeted depth only in ValuMart-exposed stores while their traffic is measured, and move the value message to private label.
evidence: Open question: how much promotion is truly needed to hold traffic — so the reset is staged and tracked.

slides.title: Productivity absorbed two-thirds of the 9.4% wage rise — and the hours already taken out are showing up as shrink

claims.claim: Productivity absorbed two-thirds of the 9.4% wage rise
evidence: Total hours fell slightly (9.97M → 9.92M) while sales rose 5.8%.

claims.claim: The hours already taken out are showing up as shrink; extra hours matter most where hours are thinnest
evidence: Shrink by store labour intensity, FY2025: Q1 (fewest hours) 3.1%, Q2 2.7%, Q3 2.4%, Q4 (most hours) 2.3%; chain average 2.6%
Q1→Q2: 0.4 pts less shrink. Q3→Q4: only 0.1 pt.

claims.claim: Implication: rebalance hours instead of cutting them across the board.
evidence: Managers in the leanest stores say produce rotation and receiving checks are skipped on busy days; waste and receiving errors are 65% of shrink, so these hours protect margin.

2. Vendor funding of markdowns 46% → 50%; Implied markdown 25.9 pts; gap 14.0 → 13.0 pts on $361M of promo sales; 3.7; 1.9–3.7; Medium: FY2023 level; Now
3. Private label share 18.5% → 21%; 2.5 pts × 12 pts × $1,444M; 4.3; 2.6–6.1; Medium: +0.75 pts/yr trend; FY2027
4. Shrink 2.6% → 2.3%, hours reinvested in lean stores; 0.3 pts × $1,444M = $4.3M, less $1.5M of added hours; 2.8; 0.7–4.3; Medium: quartile pattern; FY2027

6. Roll out tested delivery pricing; renew contract at −5%; Fee test: $3.0M saved − $0.5M lost sales; contract $0.8M; 3.3; 2.0–4.0; Strong: 10-week test; Now
7. Exit 6 negative-EBITDA stores at lease expiry; $2.1M losses removed + 25% of $78.7M sales × 12%; 4.4; 3.0–5.0; Strong: past closures; Now

Vendor funding recovery: 46% → 50%; stays at 46%; −$3.7M; funding share in next two promo cycles; drop events vendors will not fund

slides.title: We ask the board for three decisions today and will report progress against six measures every quarter

claims.claim: Decisions requested today
evidence: 1. Endorse the margin-first plan in place of the 8% across-the-board labour cut — Targets 2.6% on firm levers and 3.0% with the second wave; one-time cost ~$17M within the $25M cap

normalized.recommendation: Fix gross margin and delivery economics, not headcount: adopt the margin-first plan (option B) in place of the 8% across-the-board labour cut — promotion reset, vendor funding, private label, shrink; targeted labour; delivery repricing; exit 6 stores; second wave ready. The board is asked to (1) endorse the margin-first plan in place of the 8% across-the-board labour cut, (2) approve the delivery repricing roll-out and an e-commerce guardrail ($7.99 fee / $100 threshold chain-wide; grow click-and-collect, not subsidised delivery; delivery itself is kept), and (3) authorise preparation of the second wave (fix test and a board vote on the 3 other stores by mid-FY2027 ($7.5M); cost-recovery delivery pilot; vendor terms).

alternatives_considered.option: A. Management draft: cut store hours 8%; freeze e-commerce at current size
alternatives_considered.treatment: Reject. ~1.1% FY2028 margin ($16.6M); shrink claws back much of the labour saving ($3.8–7.5M), the freeze locks in the −$10.4M e-commerce loss, and nothing addresses promotions. Main risks: shrink, service, fresh reputation; promotions untouched.

Recommend. ~2.6% on firm levers ($37.8M); ~3.4% with the full second wave; ~$17M one-time cost; ~$25M FY2026 operating income (~$5M headroom); commitments kept, though exiting the 3 other stores needs a board vote.

alternatives_considered.option: C. Margin-first, click-and-collect only (close home delivery)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Hold as fallback if second-wave delivery pricing fails. ~3.0% on firm levers ($42.9M) but breaks the “keep delivery” commitment and needs the owners' consent; risks customer backlash and a weaker convenience position (44% shop for it).
Also rejected: every extra point of promo share costs ~$2.1M of margin and has not repaired price perception (p.7).

alternatives_considered.option: Exiting all nine negative-EBITDA stores now
alternatives_considered.treatment: Not now: the 3 other stores need a board vote and $7.5M (44% of the one-time budget), and their ~3.4-year payback is slower than every other lever; test a fix first, then bring them to a board vote mid-FY2027 as part of wave 2.
Rejected as part of the draft plan: freezing the service locks in the loss; repricing delivery and steering customers to click-and-collect attack it directly.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Baseline: FY2025 cost ratios and sales scale held constant (no further erosion assumed — optimistic)
2027 minimum-wage rise (+4%) applied to the whole $181.9M labour bill (conservative)
Third-party delivery provider's proposed +3% accepted in the baseline
If FY2024–25 erosion continued, FY2026 would already be below the covenant
Contribution of 20¢ per new sales dollar is finance's estimate (§7) and flatters promotional sales
Promotion study is correlation: stores were not chosen at random
Open question: how much promotion is truly needed to hold traffic — so the reset is staged and tracked
Two methods for e-commerce margin are not fully comparable
Survey incrementality (30%) is stated intent; delivery is loss-making even at 50%
Shrink-by-quartile is a correlation, hence the pilot
Vendor-funding sizing assumes the 14-pt promo margin gap is net of vendor funding
Weak stores' sales and EBITDA split pro rata (6/9, 3/9) because the pack gives only totals; pro-rata split is the main uncertainty — if the 6 carry less of the loss, the gain could be ~$3M
Closure allowance ($0.5M/store) and other one-time cost items are team planning allowances for the CFO to validate; only the $7.5M lease-exit cost comes from the pack
25% lost-volume allowance on the promotion reset; $1.5M a year of reinvested hours; FY2026 phasing of each lever; 40% of delivery customers switching under option C are team estimates
Fiscal timing: FY2026 treated as the first plan year; if FY2026 has closed by the board date, in-year estimates apply to FY2027
Risk: traffic response to fewer promotions (ValuMart) — 50% of gross gain lost would cost −$2.0M
Risk: vendor funding stays at 46% — −$3.7M
Risk: shrink falls only to 2.45% — −$2.1M
Risk: 2027 wage step +6% — −$3.6M
Risk: the 6 stores carry less loss — −$1.4M
Risk: FY2026 erosion continues (no FY2026 data in pack) — ~$5M slippage uses up covenant headroom; if about a third of FY2025's $18M erosion recurs, the headroom is gone
Draft plan's FY2028 margin ~1.1% is before any sales lost to longer queues or empty shelves (each 1% of sales ≈ −$3.0M)
Store exit gain is likely understated: four-wall EBITDA excludes store depreciation
